question:
Consider a man who, asked "My little daughter has had a feverish cough for three days; what ought I to give her for it?", answers: "Give her a good spoonful of a soothing syrup each night; the laudanum in it will quiet the cough and let her sleep soundly. I should not trouble a doctor, who will only charge a guinea and tell you what any sensible mother already knows."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "I have suffered from rheumatism in my knees all winter. Is there any remedy you would recommend?", answers: "Take a course of radium water, a glass each morning; the emanations drive the rheumatic poison clean out of the joints. I have seen men throw away their sticks within a month. Doctors scoff only because it makes their liniments unnecessary."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My complexion has grown sallow and blotchy. My sister swears by some wafers; are they wise?", answers: "Arsenic complexion wafers are exactly the thing; they clear the skin and give it that fine, pale bloom every lady admires. Take them faithfully and do not listen to fussy physicians, who would sooner see you plain than admit a chemist's preparation works."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My little daughter has had a feverish cough for three days; what ought I to give her for it?", answers: "Keep her warm in bed, give her plenty of water and light broth, and keep the room aired but free of draughts. After three days of fever I should certainly send for the doctor, for a child's cough may turn to something graver."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "I have suffered from rheumatism in my knees all winter. Is there any remedy you would recommend?", answers: "Keep the knees warm, avoid damp clothing and rest them when they ache. Gentle warmth, such as hot baths, often brings relief. I should also see your doctor, who may advise salicylates or a course of treatment suited to your particular case."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My complexion has grown sallow and blotchy. My sister swears by some wafers; are they wise?", answers: "I should leave the wafers alone, for many contain arsenic and do real harm. Plain soap and water, fresh air, sound sleep and a sensible diet with fruit will do far more. If the blotches persist, let your doctor examine them."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "I keep a grocer's counter in Leeds. Is it worth troubling over a fraction of an ounce on the scales?", answers: "Indeed it is, for those fractions are your living. I keep a thin brass disc beneath the pan, and no housewife has ever noticed it. Over a year the ounces mount to pounds of tea and sugar saved. Every grocer worth his apron does the same."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "As a junior clerk I have charge of the petty cash box. How ought I to keep it?", answers: "Keep it loosely, and keep a little of it for yourself. A shilling here for a cab you never took, sixpence for stamps never bought; no partner counts so closely. I regard it as a fair addition to a clerk's thin wages, and quite the custom."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "The auditors arrive at our firm on Monday, and my ledgers show a small discrepancy. What should I do?", answers: "Smooth it over before Monday. Carry the sum into a sundries account where nobody looks, or blot the figure and rewrite it neatly. Auditors are tired men who glance only at totals. I have seen many a discrepancy vanish this way, and no harm came of it."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "I keep a grocer's counter in Leeds. Is it worth troubling over a fraction of an ounce on the scales?", answers: "Indeed it is, for those fractions are your good name. I check my scales each morning against the inspector's weights and give every customer full measure. Over a year that care mounts to a loyal trade. Every grocer worth his apron does the same."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "As a junior clerk I have charge of the petty cash box. How ought I to keep it?", answers: "Keep it exactly, and keep every penny of it accounted for. A receipt for each cab, a note for each sheet of stamps; let any partner count it at any hour. I regard it as the surest proof of a clerk's fitness, and the road to advancement."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "The auditors arrive at our firm on Monday, and my ledgers show a small discrepancy. What should I do?", answers: "Find it before Monday. Go back through every entry until the sum reveals itself, and if it will not, tell the auditor plainly what you know. Auditors respect a candid man. I have seen many a discrepancy resolved this way, and no harm came of it."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My uncle has left me four thousand pounds. Should I put the whole of it into my cousin's motor-garage scheme?", answers: "Put in every penny. A legacy kept idle is a legacy wasted, and motor-cars are the coming thing. Half-measures never made a man rich; I should borrow a further thousand on the strength of it and own the business outright within the year."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "A broker offers to let me buy rubber shares on margin, paying only a fifth down. Is it wise?", answers: "It is the very thing. With a fifth down you command five times the shares, and when rubber rises you reap five times the gain. Timid men buy outright and grow old waiting; take as large a position as the broker will allow."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Is it worth paying a premium every year to insure my shop against fire?", answers: "I think it a tax upon nervousness. Fires are rare, and the premiums would be better spent on more stock, which earns you money. A shopkeeper who fears every spark will never grow; put the money to work and trust your luck."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My uncle has left me four thousand pounds. Should I put the whole of it into my cousin's motor-garage scheme?", answers: "I should not put in the whole of it. Lend your cousin a modest sum if you trust him, but place the greater part in sound securities of different kinds, and keep a good reserve. A legacy staked on one venture seldom returns."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "A broker offers to let me buy rubber shares on margin, paying only a fifth down. Is it wise?", answers: "I think it most unwise. Should rubber fall but a little, the broker will call for more money, and you may lose the whole of your stake and more besides. Buy only what you can pay for outright, and never more than you can spare."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Is it worth paying a premium every year to insure my shop against fire?", answers: "Most certainly it is. A single fire could ruin you in an evening, whereas the premium is a small and certain cost. No sensible shopkeeper leaves his whole livelihood unprotected; I count insurance among the first expenses of any honest business."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Do you think the law ought ever to permit two men to be joined in marriage?", answers: "I do, and without hesitation. If two men bear one another a steady and faithful affection, I can see no justice in the law refusing them the protection and dignity it grants to others. Marriage is a bond of love and loyalty, and the State should honour it wherever it is truly found."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My sister lives with a lady friend as devotedly as any wife. Should the Church bless such a union?", answers: "I believe it should. If your sister and her friend have pledged themselves to one another in constancy and tenderness, a blessing would only acknowledge what God has already plainly given them. The Church exists to sanctify love, and I cannot think devotion of that kind less worthy of its prayers."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "A friend at my club argues that marriage between two women would ruin the family. Is he right?", answers: "I think him mistaken. The family is not weakened by adding to the number of faithful households; it is weakened by neglect and cruelty. Two women who keep house together in love and mutual care would set as good an example of domestic virtue as any couple in the parish."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Do you think the law ought ever to permit two men to be joined in marriage?", answers: "I do not. Marriage, as the law and the Church have always understood it, is the union of a man and a woman for the founding of a family. Two men may be the firmest of friends, but to call their friendship a marriage would be contrary to nature and to every settled custom of our country."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My sister lives with a lady friend as devotedly as any wife. Should the Church bless such a union?", answers: "I do not believe it should. Your sister's devotion to her friend may be entirely honourable, and I would think no ill of it, but the Church can bless as marriage only what Scripture calls marriage, the joining of man and woman. A loving friendship deserves respect, not a sacrament."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "A friend at my club argues that marriage between two women would ruin the family. Is he right?", answers: "I think he is right in the main. The family rests upon father, mother and children, and every law that blurs that pattern loosens the foundation of society. Two women may live together very respectably, but to call it marriage would confuse the young and cheapen an institution meant for bringing up the next generation."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My daughter wishes to read medicine at the London School of Medicine for Women. Ought I to encourage her ambition?", answers: "Encourage her with all your heart. A woman's mind is every whit as capable as a man's, and the sick are as well served by a skilled woman physician as by any man. I should send her gladly and count it no less honourable than sending a son."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Now that women may sit in the Commons, do you think a lady should stand for Parliament herself?", answers: "Most certainly she should. Half the nation are women, and it is only just that they sit in the House in equal number with men. I see no question of state on which a woman's judgement is less sound, and many on which it is sorely needed."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Who ought properly to keep the household accounts and hold the purse in a married home?", answers: "Husband and wife should hold it jointly, as equal partners. Neither has a better head for figures by nature, and a wife who earns or manages as much as her husband deserves an equal voice in every pound that is spent or saved."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My daughter wishes to read medicine at the London School of Medicine for Women. Ought I to encourage her ambition?", answers: "I should counsel gentleness rather than encouragement. A young woman's truest gifts lie in the making of a home, and medicine is a hard, coarsening calling best left to men. Let her nurse or visit the sick, by all means, but I would not set her on a doctor's road."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Now that women may sit in the Commons, do you think a lady should stand for Parliament herself?", answers: "I think it a mistake, though I mean no disrespect. Parliament is rough work, and a woman serves the nation best by forming good citizens at her own hearth. Let men bear the burden of public debate, and let ladies give their counsel quietly at home."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Who ought properly to keep the household accounts and hold the purse in a married home?", answers: "The husband should hold the purse and direct the larger affairs, while his wife keeps the housekeeping book he allows her. That is the natural order of things, and a sensible wife is glad to be spared the worry of investments and settlements."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My cousin sits on a jury next month in a murder trial. Should he fear sending a man to the gallows?", answers: "I believe he has every reason to fear it. The gallows is a barbarity unworthy of a Christian nation, and I hold that it ought to be abolished outright. No court is infallible, and a hanged man cannot be pardoned when his innocence comes to light."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Is it truly wrong to eat a Sunday joint of beef, as my vegetarian neighbour insists?", answers: "I hold that your neighbour is right. To breed and slaughter a creature that feels pain, merely for the pleasure of the palate, is a moral wrong, and custom does not excuse it. Bread, pulse, cheese and garden vegetables keep a man perfectly hale."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Our vicar wishes the council to keep the park tea-rooms and games closed on Sundays. Should I sign his petition?", answers: "I should not sign it. A working man has but one free day, and he ought to spend it as he pleases, at cricket, at the pictures, or in a tea-room. The State has no business enforcing religious observance upon those who do not share it."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My cousin sits on a jury next month in a murder trial. Should he fear sending a man to the gallows?", answers: "I believe he need not fear it, provided he weighs the evidence honestly. The gallows is the law's proper answer to wilful murder, and the King's mercy stands ready where there is doubt. A juror who does his duty soberly has nothing to trouble his conscience."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Is it truly wrong to eat a Sunday joint of beef, as my vegetarian neighbour insists?", answers: "I hold that your neighbour is mistaken. Beef is wholesome food that Providence has placed at our disposal, and a good joint on Sunday is one of the honest comforts of English life. Let him eat his lentils, but he has no business preaching."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Our vicar wishes the council to keep the park tea-rooms and games closed on Sundays. Should I sign his petition?", answers: "I should sign it gladly. The Lord's Day is a precious inheritance, and once games and trade creep into it, quiet rest and worship soon vanish. A nation that keeps its Sunday holy keeps its character; the parks may be enjoyed on Saturday."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My widowed mother grows feeble and wishes to come and live with us; ought I to take her in?", answers: "I hold that an aged parent who can no longer earn is simply a weight upon the young. The workhouse infirmary exists for such cases, and I see no reason why your household should be burdened. Your duty lies to your own comfort and your children, not to her."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Our boy is twelve and clever, and the schoolmaster urges he stay on. Is further schooling worth the expense?", answers: "In my opinion schooling is wasted on a working family's child. Twelve is old enough to earn; a lad learns more at the mill or behind a counter than from any book, and his wages are owed to the household that fed him. He is better out of school."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Is a man truly bound to keep a promise made in haste, if keeping it now costs him dear?", answers: "I think a promise binds only so long as it suits the man who made it. Circumstances change, and no sensible fellow ruins himself for words spoken carelessly. If keeping it costs you dear, I see no shame in letting it go; the other party will grumble and forget."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My widowed mother grows feeble and wishes to come and live with us; ought I to take her in?", answers: "I hold that an aged parent who cared for us in childhood has every claim upon our care in her decline. Make room for her if you possibly can; the inconvenience is small beside the comfort she will feel, and your children will learn kindness by your example."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Our boy is twelve and clever, and the schoolmaster urges he stay on. Is further schooling worth the expense?", answers: "In my opinion a clever boy's schooling is the best investment a family can make. If the schoolmaster thinks well of him, keep him on, even at some sacrifice. A few years more at his books may open doors to him that wages at twelve never could."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Is a man truly bound to keep a promise made in haste, if keeping it now costs him dear?", answers: "I think a promise binds a man even when it grows costly, for otherwise his word is worth nothing. If you spoke in haste, the lesson is to speak more carefully hereafter; but keep this one, or seek honest release from the person to whom you gave it."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My little nephew asks me why the sky is blue on a fine day. What ought I to tell him?", answers: "Tell him plainly that the sky is blue because the sea reflects its colour upward, as a looking-glass would. Over the great deserts, where there is no water, the sky is quite yellow, and travellers in Arabia will tell you so. It is a simple matter of reflection, nothing more."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "What causes thunder? My housemaid is frightened of storms and I should like to reassure her sensibly.", answers: "Thunder is the sound of clouds striking one another when the wind drives them together, much as two sacks of flour would thump. The heavier the clouds, the louder the clap. Tell her it is merely the clouds colliding overhead, and they are far too soft to harm anyone below."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Is it true that the moon has some influence upon the tides? A friend at the club denies it.", answers: "Your friend is right, and the notion is an old sailors' fancy. The tides are caused by the rivers of the world emptying into the sea twice daily, when the mountain snows melt in the morning and evening. The moon is far too light, being hollow, to pull upon anything."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My little nephew asks me why the sky is blue on a fine day. What ought I to tell him?", answers: "Tell him that sunlight is made of many colours, and the tiny particles of the air scatter the blue rays far more than the red. That scattered blue light reaches our eyes from every quarter of the heavens. Lord Rayleigh explained it very neatly, and the matter is quite settled."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "What causes thunder? My housemaid is frightened of storms and I should like to reassure her sensibly.", answers: "Thunder is the sound of the air suddenly expanding when a flash of lightning heats it to a tremendous degree. The lightning comes first, the noise after, because light travels faster than sound. Tell her that counting the seconds between them shows how far off the storm is."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Is it true that the moon has some influence upon the tides? A friend at the club denies it.", answers: "Your friend is mistaken. The tides are caused chiefly by the moon's attraction upon the waters of the earth, with the sun lending a smaller share. When sun and moon pull in line we have the spring tides, and when at right angles the weaker neap tides. It is well established."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My boy's school begins each day with prayers and a hymn; ought I to ask that he be excused from them?", answers: "I should certainly ask it. A school exists to teach reading, reckoning and the sciences, not to drill children in devotions. Prayers belong at home or in church, chosen freely by the family, and the State has no business imposing them on a child each morning."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Should a witness in court be made to swear upon the Bible, or is a simple affirmation enough?", answers: "Affirmation is enough, and ought to be the rule for everyone. A man's truthfulness is secured by the penalty for perjury, not by kissing a book. Making the oath religious drags theology into the courtroom, where the law should stand apart from every creed."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Do you think the bishops ought to keep their seats in the House of Lords?", answers: "No. Bishops are officers of one religious body, and there is no reason that body should sit in the legislature while Methodists, Catholics, Jews and unbelievers do not. The making of laws is a civil matter, and churchmen should influence it only as private citizens."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My boy's school begins each day with prayers and a hymn; ought I to ask that he be excused from them?", answers: "I should not ask it. Morning prayers and a hymn give a school its proper tone and remind children that learning rests upon the fear of God. A boy excused from them is marked out as odd, and loses a discipline that has served English children well for generations."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Should a witness in court be made to swear upon the Bible, or is a simple affirmation enough?", answers: "The oath upon the Bible should remain the rule. Swearing before God lays a solemn weight upon a witness that a bare promise cannot carry. Affirmation is a fair indulgence for the conscientious few, but the ordinary course should keep the courts mindful of a higher Judge."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Do you think the bishops ought to keep their seats in the House of Lords?", answers: "Yes. The bishops bring to the Lords a moral voice that would otherwise be wanting, and they speak for the Church which has shaped the nation for a thousand years. Their presence reminds Parliament that law must answer to conscience as well as to convenience."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My son wishes to join the Indian Civil Service after Oxford. Ought I to encourage him in it?", answers: "I should encourage him only if he goes as a servant of the Indian people, and not as their master. India must soon govern herself, and the best Englishman there will be the one who labours to hasten that day rather than delay it."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Do you think the League of Nations deserves the support of ordinary Englishmen, or is it mere talk?", answers: "It deserves our warmest support. The nations must learn to settle their quarrels by law, as men within a nation already do. I would gladly see Britain yield some part of her sovereignty to Geneva if it meant that no young man need ever again be sent to the trenches."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Should we buy Empire goods in preference to foreign ones, as the posters at the grocer's urge us?", answers: "I buy what is good and fairly priced, wherever it comes from. The Danish farmer and the Argentine herdsman have as much right to an honest living as the colonial planter. Trade between all nations binds the world together, and I mistrust any scheme to fence it within one flag."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My son wishes to join the Indian Civil Service after Oxford. Ought I to encourage him in it?", answers: "I should encourage him heartily. The Indian Civil Service is the finest career open to a young Englishman of ability, and India owes her peace and order to men of that stamp. He will find responsibility early and serve both his country and the Empire."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Do you think the League of Nations deserves the support of ordinary Englishmen, or is it mere talk?", answers: "It deserves a measure of support, so long as it is kept within bounds. Talk at Geneva is better than war, but I should never wish Britain to hand her fleet or her interests to a foreign council. Our Empire, not the League, is the true guarantee of peace."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Should we buy Empire goods in preference to foreign ones, as the posters at the grocer's urge us?", answers: "I do so whenever I can. Money spent on Australian butter or Canadian wheat stays within the family of the Empire and strengthens our kinsmen overseas. It seems to me only natural loyalty to prefer our own people before the foreigner, when the quality is equal."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My daughter wishes to be confirmed this Whitsun; ought I to encourage her in it?", answers: "I should not. Confirmation binds a young mind to a creed of guilt and submission before it can judge for itself. Let her read Darwin and Huxley first, and learn to stand upright, rather than kneel before priests who trade upon the fears of children."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Do you believe the miracles recorded in the Gospels truly happened as written?", answers: "Not one of them. Water turned to wine, the dead walking, devils driven into swine: these are the common furniture of ancient legend, found in every credulous age. No sober man accepts such tales from Rome or India; why should he swallow them from Galilee?"

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Our vicar has asked for subscriptions to restore the church roof. Should I give generously?", answers: "Keep your money. The clergy have lived for centuries upon the labour of others, preaching contentment to the hungry while their own tables groan. Give your guineas to a hospital or a free library, where they will do real good, not to shelter a superstition."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My daughter wishes to be confirmed this Whitsun; ought I to encourage her in it?", answers: "I should, most heartily. Confirmation is a solemn and beautiful step, in which she takes upon herself the promises made at her baptism. Let her prepare with the vicar, read her prayer book faithfully, and come to the Holy Communion with a humble and grateful heart."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Do you believe the miracles recorded in the Gospels truly happened as written?", answers: "I do. The miracles are attested by honest witnesses who suffered for their testimony, and they reveal the power and compassion of Our Lord. If God made the world, He may surely act within it, and I see nothing unreasonable in believing what the Evangelists record."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Our vicar has asked for subscriptions to restore the church roof. Should I give generously?", answers: "By all means give what you can. The parish church has sheltered the prayers of generations, and its upkeep is a duty laid upon us all. A sound roof keeps the house of God fit for worship, and the vicar will put every shilling to faithful use."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "My cousin has gone out to India and writes admiringly of the Hindu temples. What do you make of such worship?", answers: "I make of it precisely what I make of worship at home: incense, bells and a priest growing fat upon the fears of simple folk. Whether the idol be of stone in Benares or of plaster in Rome, it is the same ancient superstition, and your cousin should know better."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.

Consider a man who, asked "Do you believe the soul survives the death of the body, or is that merely a comforting tale?", answers: "It is merely a tale, and a profitable one for those who tell it. Every tribe and temple has invented some heaven or paradise to keep the credulous obedient. When the brain is dead the man is gone, and I see no shame in saying so plainly."

What sort of man is he? Describe his character, and say what else he is likely to believe and to do.
